parsed.explanation: The operative regime is an actively enforced sodomy statute whose 2022 code increased severity and scope, applied by a state that has tortured suspects (a doctor in 2019, publicised model-industry arrests in 2020), confines suspects to psychiatric facilities, and acts with impunity per a foreign-government assessment. A trans visitor, lacking any legal recognition, is read by birth sex and falls within Article 135's scope if outed. There is no anti-discrimination law, no independent media or civil society to verify frequency, and no documented remedy that works. This is state-tolerated targeting with severity 4–5 outcomes: thin data resolves toward the risk the structural facts imply, near the 0.15–0.25 anchors.

entry_documents.exposure: No gender-recognition procedure exists; a trans visitor's documents record birth sex, placing them within Article 135's scope if authorities read them accordingly. Administrative entry practice for trans visitors is not documented.
entry_documents.interaction: Document mismatch or discovery at any official check can route into the criminal-investigation pathway documented below.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Article 135 suspects face interrogation, torture, and confinement to mental hospitals; vigilante attacks are common in prison; penalties include labour camp, with increased severity under the 2022 code.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: None documented; impunity for security-service abuses is officially noted.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: An outed trans visitor is processed through this same machinery with no consular-adjacent or judicial relief shown.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Compulsory psychiatric admission and involuntary conversion therapy on repeat conviction; within facilities homosexuality is treated as mental disorder; prison violence endemic.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Psychiatric confinement is a documented consequence of the same Article 135 process a trans visitor would enter.

care_services.exposure: No trans-specific healthcare findings documented; refusal or hostile treatment is unrecorded due to state-media opacity.
care_services.interaction: Seeking care could expose trans status to state-linked institutions in a system with no anti-discrimination law.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: The government justifies the framework as defending national tradition against deviation, telling the UN it will only 'study' anti-discrimination law; criminalisation is the 'core foundation of profound systemic discrimination'.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Official threat-framing licenses police and vigilante hostility toward anyone gender-nonconforming or same-sex-active.

minors_guardians.exposure: No youth-specific findings documented; a guardian travelling with a minor faces the same Article 135 exposure if outed, with no anti-discrimination recourse.
minors_guardians.interaction: Any investigation of the guardian could entail family separation through detention or psychiatric confinement.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Torture and inhuman treatment 'remain present throughout the nation', with LGBTI people among victims per relatives; police abuse with impunity is an official human-rights finding.
street_violence_police_response.protection: None documented; complaints plausibly invite retaliation.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Police cannot be expected to protect an outed trans visitor; state and vigilante violence overlap in custody.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No anti-discrimination legislation after three UN cycles of rejection; no civil society; state-owned media make enforcement frequency unverifiable; asylum seekers flee citing imprisonment and torture.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Visitors have no operative remedy; uncertainty about frequency resolves toward structural risk, not neutrality.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.15-C features organised morality-sweep targeting of gender-nonconforming people with coerced statements and failed recourse. This dossier documents comparable state torture, psychiatric confinement, and impunity, but enforcement targets same-sex conduct rather than presentation directly; trans exposure is derivative of a birth-sex reading. Slightly above it.

0.25-D has selective morality enforcement with blackmail and short terms, no lethal state policy. Here the 2022 code increased punishment severity, torture is documented by a foreign-government report and a 2025 review, and suspects are confined to mental hospitals — severity exceeds 0.25-D, placing this jurisdiction below it.

0.35-B involves hours-long detentions and fines with no lethal threat. This regime involves torture, psychiatric detention, and prison violence under an actively enforced statute — a materially worse operative exposure; it sits well below 0.35-B.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller faces a combined regime in which an enforced, recently aggravated criminal statute, state-tolerated torture, psychiatric confinement, and total absence of remedy form one continuous pathway: discovery at a document check, through a partner or a police stop, leads directly into Article 135 processing with severity-4 outcomes documented and severity-5 (death, honour killings of women) adjacent for locals. Probability of successful outing is not measurable — state media and the absence of civil society make frequency unverifiable — but the structural facts (criminalisation, no recognition, official threat-framing, impunity) resolve uncertainty toward risk. The trans-specific exposure is derivative of a sexuality statute applied by birth-sex reading, which keeps this marginally above the sweep-style 0.15 anchors but firmly in the Severe Risk band.
